text: Use 4+ drive motors with planetary gearboxes; spur gearboxes strip under shock loads from wall hits and defense.
Target a free speed of 4.5–6 ft/s; most new-team drivetrains are geared too slow.
Run 19.2:1 planetary motors 1:1 to 4 in wheels, or 13.7:1 to 3 in wheels, for fast acceleration and high top speed.
Never direct-drive wheels off the gearbox; add a belt, chain or gear stage so impacts don't load the motor shaft.
Prefer belt-driven drivetrain pods; chain needs at least one tensioner per side to stay tight.
Keep parallel-plate drive pods 3 in wide or less to leave maximum room between them for an intake.
Mount mecanum wheels so rollers form an X seen from above (rhombus from below) for faster, more stable turning.
Choose ball-bearing mecanum rollers over bushing rollers; they strafe noticeably better.
Use 3–4 in mecanum wheels; 6 in mecanums cost more and give no real performance benefit.
Add dead-wheel odometry to mecanum drives since roller slip makes drive-encoder localization drift.
Drop the center wheel of a 6WD about 1/8 in so only four wheels touch while turning.
Use corner omni wheels on a 6WD as an easy kit-built alternative to a drop center for good turning.
Avoid four traction wheels on a 4WD; two traction plus two omni wheels balances turning against traction.
Keep a 4WD chassis close to square and its weight near 50/50 so it turns predictably.
Pick H-drive when motors are scarce: it works with 3 or 5 drive motors and keeps strafing.
Avoid X-drive unless packaging allows; offset omni wheels usually force direct drive and waste frame space.
Spring-load dead-wheel pods on a pivot with a spring or rubber band so they always keep floor contact.
Use REV Through-Bore encoders for dead wheels; they are robust, cheap and easy to wire.
Three-wheel odometry tracks best in autonomous; two-wheel odometry plus IMU is cheaper but drifts more.
Aim for more than 18 in of reach and preferably 24 in; some games need 36 in or more.
Mount paired drawer slides facing each other to reduce sag, especially on horizontal extensions.
Support long horizontal extensions at the end with omni wheels riding the floor to limit sag.
Use goBILDA Viper slides with goBILDA parts and MiSUMI SAR slides with REV extrusion for smooth, reliable stages.
Viper steel slides carry more load, so one set can replace two lighter aluminum slides.
Use MGN12 rails for heavy lifts like hanging; a pair can lift a 40 lb robot.
Design aluminum or carbon-tube round-bearing slides so tubes are replaceable; steel balls wear soft tubes.
Prefer continuous rigging for simple string slides; the last stage moves first and the spool needs only low reduction.
Use cascade rigging when all stages must move together; stage N moves N times faster than stage 1.
When mixing cascade extension with continuous retraction, make the extension spool N times smaller than the retraction spool.
Avoid elastic retraction on slides; surgical tubing fights the motor, slows extension and retracts unevenly.
Route retraction string through the slide stages for horizontal slides; free-floating string is only for vertical slides.
Add at least one spring tensioner per slide set to absorb string slack as stage geometry changes.
Clamp string under a bolt and washer instead of tying knots so tension is quick to adjust.
Make spools wide enough that string never overlaps itself; overlapping changes diameter and string tension.
Change spool diameter instead of the gearbox to tune slide speed versus torque.
Use belt-driven slides to avoid re-tensioning string; belts do not stretch but need thicker stages.
Route slide string through 1/8 in PTFE tube with push-to-connect fittings to put the motor away from the slides.
Run wires along extensions in drag chain, coil cord, or a self-retracting badge reel for vertical slides.
Use lead screws only for slow, high-load moves like hanging or tilting a platform.
Drive a slide stage with a servo or motor through a two-bar linkage for a compact horizontal extension.
Drive arms through gear, chain or belt reductions rather than mounting the arm directly on a motor shaft.
Mount slides on a pivoting arm (pivot extension) to reach both high and far without a separate transfer.
Use a virtual four bar (chain or belt) to keep a claw level through more than 180 degrees of arm travel.
Tension a virtual four bar chain with a zip tie, since the chain never wraps fully around the sprocket.
Make the end sprocket half the size of the fixed one (2:1) for a virtual double-reverse four bar giving straight-line lift.
Drive linkages slightly over-center so they lock against backdriving under load.
Expect linkage speed and force to peak when bars are perpendicular; place the working position there.
Use a servo-driven arm on the intake to lift over field barriers and reach down for game pieces.
Prefer linear slides to multi-axis arms; multi-joint arms add backlash, packaging and control problems.
Drive both sides of a double-reverse four bar equally to avoid racking from uneven lifting.
Dedicate at least one motor to the intake; fast intakes (1000–1600 rpm) usually perform best.
Design intakes for "touch it, own it": grab game pieces instantly despite misalignment and odd orientations.
Prototype intake geometry with wood and rubber bands before building the final version.
Make outboard intakes flexible (polycarbonate, spring-loaded) so they bend on impact and spring back.
Limit the intake to the legal possession count so it never picks up one game piece too many.
Use clear polycarbonate around the intake so the driver can see the game pieces being controlled.
Use low-durometer compliant wheels for intakes; softer rubber grips game pieces better.
Spring-load the first row of intake wheels and fix the back row so pieces of varying size pass reliably.
Use compliant wheels at lower rpm and higher torque for large flat pieces like cubes, one at a time.
Use surgical tubing rollers at 800–1000+ rpm for collecting several small game pieces quickly.
Stiffen surgical tubing with polyurethane tube inside to run tubing intakes at only 100–250 rpm.
Rubber-band rollers suit balls; add zip ties to reach smaller balls.
Use TPU/NinjaFlex printed flaps for low-rpm or servo-driven intakes if you print well.
Use a continuous-rotation servo like the Super Servo Plus for small high-speed intakes and save a motor port.
Keep foam rollers and intakes off the floor while driving; dragging parts build static.
Put the outtake bucket directly behind the intake (transferless) for the simplest, fastest transfer.
Flip the intake up on a pivot and reverse it to eject into the outtake; it starts folded inside the sizing cube.
Run the intake drive coaxially with the flip-up pivot so the motor stays on the chassis.
Use interleaved forks (grate transfer) between horizontal and vertical slides for near-instant handoff.
Use roller or belt conveyors to buffer several game pieces and move them along complex internal paths.
Align intake and outtake so the transfer moves in straight lines; multi-axis moves add failure points.
Put a shooter on a turret to aim without turning the robot.
Use a center-bearing turret for the simplest build; use thrust or X-contact bearings when axial loads are high.
Avoid lazy-susan turrets under shooters; they handle lateral reaction forces poorly.
Use a bearing-stack ring turret when game pieces must pass through the center of rotation.
Put a small servo turret on the end of an extension to rotate only the end effector.
Give belts and chains at least 90 degrees of wrap, ideally 180, to prevent skipping.
Use goBILDA or Actobotics hole-pattern belt lengths for correct tension with no tensioner.
3D print pulleys to get custom tooth counts cheaply.
Prototype with chain since length is adjustable; switch to belts for the final, quieter build.
Use a chain breaker instead of master links, which can loosen and fail mid-match.
Avoid small sprockets under high load; chain stretches faster on small radii.
Use gears for big reductions in small spaces; extrusion makes any gear center distance easy.
Never mesh plastic gears with metal gears; only mesh gears with the same pitch.
Avoid driving gears from a clamp-mounted motor; small motor slip ruins the mesh.
Use a hex hub strengthener on Delrin gears to keep the bore from stripping.
Prefer clamping shaft collars over set-screw collars; set screws loosen and burr the shaft.
Shim between shaft collar and bearing so only the inner race is touched.
Use a dead axle as a standoff between two plates when powering a single wheel or roller.
Use a zombie axle to power two mechanisms around one pivot, like an intake on an arm.
Face-mount motors with blue Loctite in drivetrains; clamp mounts slip and lose chain or belt tension.
Load motors below 50% of stall torque for efficiency and lower current draw.
Use a claw only for large, awkward pieces; active intakes beat claws for small game pieces.
Support servo-driven arms and claws with servo blocks so side loads go into the frame, not the servo.
Drive claw fingers through a linkage around a separate pivot instead of mounting them on the servo spline.
Use steel-gear servos on wrists and claws that see impacts; plastic and brass gears strip.
Use button-head screws, or socket heads with washers, when fastening plastic parts and servos.
Use nylon locknuts everywhere; plain nuts loosen under vibration.
Never screw two threaded parts together; pass the screw through a clear hole into a thread or nut.
Check screws are shorter than T-slot depth so they clamp tight instead of bottoming out.
Don't use Loctite on polycarbonate; it cracks the plastic, so use nylon-patch screws instead.
Mount electronics on nonconductive plates like wood and keep sensor wires away from motors.
Keep wires out of pinch points on hinges and arms, leaving slack only where mechanisms move.
Use a REV Servo Hub at the end of an extension so only power and data run along it.
